concepts.title: Declarative vs. Imperative Infrastructure
concepts.description: Kubernetes is built around describing the desired end state of your system and letting the platform continuously work to achieve it, rather than issuing a sequence of one-off commands. Internalizing this shift is the biggest mental-model change for anyone coming from ops scripting or manual server management.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between declarative and imperative approaches to managing infrastructure, with concrete examples of each.
Explain why Kubernetes manifests describe desired state rather than a sequence of steps to execute.
Predict what happens when a declarative manifest is reapplied after someone has manually changed the live object out of band.
Explain, at a high level, why a continuously-running control loop is what actually makes declarative state self-healing.
Distinguish imperative kubectl commands (kubectl create, kubectl scale) from declarative kubectl apply -f, and explain why teams standardize on the latter for anything long-lived.

sections.heading: Imperative: Say What To Do, Step by Step
sections.body:
An imperative instruction tells a system what action to perform, right now, in order: `docker run`, a shell script, or `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx` followed by `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3`. Each command is a verb aimed at the cluster's *current* state at the moment it runs. Most people start here, because it's how you'd talk a human operator through a task and how scripting languages work by default: do this, then that, then the other thing.

The problem isn't that imperative commands don't work. `kubectl scale --replicas=3` will create three Pods. The problem is what happens after the command exits. Nothing about it is still running, watching, or caring whether those three Pods exist five minutes later. If a node dies and takes two of them along, the `kubectl scale` invocation that created them is long gone and cannot notice, let alone react. Anything that keeps happening after that point has to come from a separate, persistent mechanism that keeps checking and re-asserting the desired count. That mechanism is the reconciliation control loop, covered in the next concept. For now, note that the imperative command is not it: it is a single action, not an ongoing commitment.

sections.heading: Declarative: Say What Should Be True
sections.body:
A declarative approach instead describes a *state* you want to be true, and hands that description to a system that figures out, on its own and repeatedly, what actions are needed to make reality match it:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.26
```

Running `kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml` does not mean 'create three Pods right now and be done.' `replicas: 3` is not an instruction to perform an action. It's a *constraint*: this Deployment should have three matching Pods for as long as the object exists. Kubernetes persists that desired state in etcd (its backing store), and a controller becomes permanently responsible for keeping the observed world lined up with it, not just when you typed the command but continuously, until you change or delete the Deployment. The YAML file describes an end state; it is not a transcript of steps.

sections.heading: Why This Matters: Idempotency and Self-Healing
sections.body:
Two properties follow from the declarative model, and they are the reason Kubernetes is built this way rather than as a remote-execution shell.

First, **idempotency**: reapplying the same manifest a second, third, or hundredth time has no additional effect beyond the first, assuming nothing else has changed. Compare re-running `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx`, which fails with `AlreadyExists`, because `create` only knows how to insert a brand-new object. It has no concept of 'make sure this exists.' `kubectl apply`, by contrast, is built to be safely re-run: it compares the desired configuration against what's live and changes only what needs to change.

Second, and more consequential in practice: **self-healing**. If a Pod is deleted, evicted, or lost along with its node, nothing needs to 're-run a script.' The desired state (three replicas) was never a one-time instruction. It's a standing constraint that a controller keeps checking against reality. The moment observed reality (two replicas) stops matching desired state (three), the controller notices and corrects it, with no human intervention and no re-invocation of anything. This is the mechanism behind Kubernetes' resilience to node failures, and it exists because desired state is persisted and continuously enforced, instead of being an instruction that evaporates when the command that issued it exits.

sections.heading: The Practical Edge Case: Drift and Out-of-Band Changes
sections.body:
The declarative model has a sharp edge that catches nearly everyone once: `kubectl apply` doesn't compute a simple two-way diff between your file and the live object. It performs a three-way merge, comparing (1) the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation, a record of what you applied *last time*, against (2) the object's current live state and (3) the new file you're applying now. That lets `apply` remove a field you deleted from your YAML without clobbering fields something else added out of band, such as a mutating webhook, or the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusting `.spec.replicas`.

Now the sharp edge. A teammate runs `kubectl edit deployment web` and bumps `replicas` to 5, a live edit that exists in no file. Then anyone, including an automated pipeline, reapplies the *original* YAML that still says `replicas: 3`, and the count drops back to 3 with no warning. As far as `apply` is concerned, the file is the intended truth, the manual edit was never recorded in the last-applied configuration, and the live 5 is drift to be corrected back to the declared value. This is not a bug; it follows from having a single source of truth. The practical lesson: in any cluster managed declaratively (especially via GitOps), treat `kubectl edit` as a debugging tool, never as a way to make a change that should persist. Change the file, then apply it, or the next routine apply will erase your manual fix. To preview what an apply would change before running it, use `kubectl diff -f web-deployment.yaml`; it surfaces drift like this without touching the cluster.

examples.title: Imperative: A Sequence of Commands
examples.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.26
examples.explanation: Each of these commands performs one action against whatever the cluster's live state is at that moment. Nothing outside the live objects records 'the desired image is nginx:1.26 and the desired count is 3' as an inspectable artifact, so to learn what's supposed to be running you have to ask the cluster (`kubectl get deployment web -o yaml`). If you wanted to know why the Deployment ended up configured this way, or revert the image change, there's no file to diff, no pull request to review, and no commit history. The only record of intent is scattered across whichever commands were typed, in whatever order, by whoever was at a terminal. Declarative manifests close that gap.

examples.title: Declarative: The Same End State, Described Instead of Commanded
examples.code:
# web-deployment.yaml declares: this Deployment should have 3 replicas of nginx:1.26
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Running it again with the SAME file is a no-op: nothing changes, no error
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Compare: running the imperative 'create' twice fails outright
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
# Error from server (AlreadyExists): deployments.apps "web" already exists
examples.explanation: The first `apply` works out which create/patch calls are needed to bring the cluster in line with the YAML file, and issues them. The second, identical `apply` finds nothing to change and does nothing. That's idempotency, and it's what makes it safe to run `kubectl apply -f .` repeatedly in CI/CD pipelines, cron jobs, or GitOps reconcile loops without duplicate side effects. `kubectl create`, by contrast, only knows how to insert a new object, so calling it twice with the same name is an error, not a no-op. That difference is why `apply`, not `create`, is the standard entry point for anything managed as code.

examples.title: The Drift Trap: A Manual Edit Gets Silently Erased
examples.code:
# Someone manually bumps replicas to 5 on the live object
kubectl edit deployment web
# ... they type replicas: 5 and save; kubectl confirms 'deployment.apps/web edited'

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 5

# An hour later, an automated pipeline reapplies the ORIGINAL, unmodified file (still replicas: 3)
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 3 (the manual bump to 5 is gone, with no warning)
examples.explanation: The manual `kubectl edit` never touched the YAML file on disk, so from `apply`'s point of view the declared truth was always `replicas: 3`. The live 5 was drift, a discrepancy between what's declared and what's running, and `apply` resolves that kind of discrepancy in favor of the file. That is why teams relying on the declarative model treat the version-controlled manifest as the only legitimate source of truth, and treat a `kubectl edit` on a cluster with automated reconciliation as a temporary debugging measure that the next apply will revert.

misconceptions.description: Declarative just means writing YAML files instead of typing commands -- it's a syntax preference, not a behavioral difference.
misconceptions.clarification: It isn't about syntax. You could write an imperative bash script that generates and applies YAML, and the approach would still be imperative. What matters is what gets persisted as the authoritative source of truth, and whether something keeps enforcing it afterward. A declarative manifest, once applied, leaves behind a standing description that a controller re-asserts indefinitely, correcting drift and surviving node failures without re-invocation. An imperative script achieves a state once and then exits, and nothing watches afterward.

misconceptions.description: kubectl apply just computes a simple diff between my YAML file and whatever is currently running, and patches only the differences -- a straightforward two-way comparison.
misconceptions.clarification: It's a three-way merge: kubectl compares the new file, the object's live state, and a stored annotation (kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration) recording what was applied last time. That is what lets apply delete a field you removed from your YAML between applies while leaving alone a field that another actor (a mutating webhook, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, another controller) added or changed out of band. A plain two-way diff against only the live object couldn't distinguish 'this field is missing from my file because I deleted it' from 'this field was never mine to manage.'

exercises.prompt: You apply a Deployment manifest with `replicas: 2`. Later, without touching the file, you run `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5`. An hour after that, a teammate reapplies the original, unmodified YAML file (still `replicas: 2`). What is the replica count immediately after that second apply, and why?
exercises.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # file says replicas: 2
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?

# ...an hour later...
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # SAME file, still says replicas: 2
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?
hints: kubectl scale changes the live object's spec.replicas field directly -- does it write anything back to the YAML file on disk?
When kubectl apply decides what the replica count 'should' be, what does it treat as the source of truth: whatever the live object currently says, or whatever the file being applied says?
Is the scale-to-5 change recorded anywhere that the second apply would look, such as the last-applied-configuration annotation?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Right after the scale command, the count is 5. After the second apply, the count drops back to 2: the file was never updated to reflect the scale, so apply treats 2 as the declared truth and corrects the drift.
exercises.solutionExplanation: kubectl scale is an imperative action: it patches spec.replicas on the live object, giving an immediate count of 5, but it never touches web-deployment.yaml or the last-applied-configuration annotation that apply consults. When the unmodified file (still declaring replicas: 2) is reapplied an hour later, apply computes what must change to match the file, finds the live 5 differs from the declared 2, and patches it back down to 2, erasing the manual scale. This is the same drift correction that overwrites a manual kubectl edit: whatever isn't captured in the file the automation applies gets corrected, not preserved.

exercises.prompt: This deploy script is run by a CI pipeline on every merge to main. The first run succeeds. Every run after that fails with 'Error from server (AlreadyExists)'. Find and fix the bug so repeated runs are safe.
hints: kubectl create and kubectl apply are not interchangeable verbs, even though both can bring an object into existence the first time.

One of these commands has diffing logic built in and is specifically designed to be safely re-run; the other only knows how to insert a brand-new object and has no notion of 'update if it already exists.'
Which verb would you use for something you expect to run repeatedly against a source-controlled file, as opposed to a true one-time setup step?
exercises.solutionExplanation: kubectl create has no diffing or reconciliation logic. It issues a single 'insert this object' request, and if an object with that name already exists the API server rejects it with AlreadyExists, because create was never designed for 'this might already exist and that's fine.' kubectl apply is built for repeated invocation: it compares the live object with the file and sends a patch instead of an insert when the object exists, which makes it a no-op on repeated runs with an unchanged file. Swapping create for apply is why teams standardize on apply for anything driven by a CI pipeline or GitOps controller.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'I don't see the point of writing YAML manifests -- I can just write a bash script with the exact kubectl commands needed, and it's more readable.' What is the most important capability they would lose by doing that?
options: The cluster would continuously and automatically re-enforce the desired state encoded in a manifest (for example, restoring the replica count after a node failure) with nobody re-running anything; a one-time script has no ongoing effect after it exits.
YAML is mandatory because the Kubernetes API only accepts requests formatted as YAML directly on the wire.
Nothing meaningful is lost -- it's purely a matter of personal taste and code readability.
Bash scripts can't create Kubernetes objects at all -- only kubectl apply -f can talk to the API server.
assessments.explanation: The value of a declarative manifest isn't its file format. It's that the desired state gets persisted and continuously reconciled by a controller for as long as the object exists, which is what makes Kubernetes self-healing after failures. A one-off imperative script, however written, achieves a state when it runs and then has no further effect; nothing is left watching. The “Bash scripts can't create Kubernetes objects…” option is false: a script full of kubectl commands creates objects fine. The “YAML is mandatory because the Kubernetes API…” option is false: the API server's native encodings are JSON and protobuf, and YAML is a convenience format that kubectl converts client-side. The “Nothing meaningful is lost -- it's purely…” option misses the point: the difference is behavioral (ongoing reconciliation vs. one-time action), not stylistic.

assessments.prompt: kubectl apply uses a three-way strategic merge rather than a simple two-way diff between the YAML file and the live object. What is the third input to that merge, and what specific problem does including it solve?
options: The third input is a complete audit log of every kubectl command ever run against the object; it lets apply revert any change made by kubectl edit.
The third input is the object's resourceVersion; it lets apply detect concurrent writers and reject the apply outright with a conflict error.
The third input is the previous git commit hash of the file; it lets apply detect whether the file was renamed since the last commit.

The third input is the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation recording what was applied last time; it lets apply distinguish a field you deleted from your file from a field some other actor (a webhook, the HPA) added out of band, which a live-object-only diff couldn't tell apart.
assessments.explanation: A plain two-way diff between the new file and the live object can't tell 'this field is missing from my file because I deleted it' from 'this field was never mine to manage.' The last-applied-configuration annotation resolves that ambiguity by recording what the file declared last time, so apply can compare all three: a field in last-applied but missing from the new file gets removed, and a field never in last-applied is left alone even if it's on the live object. None of the other options describe a mechanism apply uses. There is no git-hash comparison and no audit-log replay, and while resourceVersion is used elsewhere for optimistic concurrency, it is not the third input to the merge.

assessments.prompt: A pipeline runs `kubectl create -f service.yaml` on every deploy and fails with `AlreadyExists` on the second and every subsequent run. If the pipeline instead ran `kubectl apply -f service.yaml` with the exact same unchanged file every time, what would happen on the second run?
options: It would succeed, but only by first deleting and then recreating the object from scratch, causing a brief outage on every single run.
It would succeed and change nothing, because apply diffs the file against the live state and the last-applied-configuration annotation, finds no difference, and effectively applies an empty patch.
It would also fail with AlreadyExists, because both create and apply refuse to touch an object that already exists.
It would succeed only if a --force flag were also passed; without it, apply behaves identically to create when the object already exists, so the second run would fail with an AlreadyExists error.
assessments.explanation: This is the idempotency that distinguishes apply from create: create has no diffing logic and always attempts a raw insert, so it fails once an object with that name exists. apply computes what needs to change and sends a no-op patch when nothing has, which is why it's safe to run repeatedly in a CI pipeline. The “It would succeed, but only by first…” option describes delete-and-recreate, which apply doesn't use for ordinary field changes, let alone a no-op; the “It would succeed only if a --force…” option is wrong because apply on an unchanged file needs no special flag.

assessments.prompt: A Deployment's YAML omits spec.replicas entirely, and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is separately adjusting the live replica count based on load. While the HPA currently has it scaled to 8, someone reapplies the exact same file (still with no replicas field). What happens to the replica count?
options: apply resets replicas back to the Kubernetes default of 1, since the field is absent from the file and the file is treated as the source of truth for everything, and the autoscaler then has to scale the Deployment back up again.
apply and the HPA immediately enter a fight, alternately setting replicas to 1 and then 8 on every reconciliation pass.

apply leaves the HPA-managed replica count of 8 untouched, because the three-way merge sees that replicas was never part of the last-applied-configuration this file manages, so there is nothing to correct or remove.
apply fails outright, refusing to proceed because the live object's replicas value doesn't match anything recorded in the file.
assessments.explanation: The three-way merge only reconciles fields that appeared in a previous last-applied-configuration. Since this file never declared replicas, apply never claimed that field, has nothing to diff or correct, and leaves the HPA's value alone. That is how apply coexists with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and other out-of-band actors: it only touches fields it manages. (One caveat: if an earlier version of the file did declare replicas and a later one drops it, the first apply after the removal does reset the count to the default of 1.) The “apply resets replicas back to the Kubernetes…” option describes a naive two-way diff against a default value, not the real three-way merge; the “apply fails outright, refusing to proceed…” and “apply and the HPA immediately enter…” options describe failure modes that don't occur in practice.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer asks why Kubernetes 'bothers' with a declarative model instead of just running a deployment script the way it's traditionally done in server ops. Explain the core motivation, and walk through at least one concrete failure scenario where the difference actually matters in practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: A traditional deployment script performs a sequence of actions once, when it runs, and then has no further effect. Nothing about it is still active five minutes later, watching for problems or correcting them. Kubernetes takes a different approach: instead of scripting steps, you write a manifest describing a *state* you want to be true (for example, 'this Deployment should always have 3 replicas of this Pod template'), and that description is persisted in the cluster's backing store, not executed and discarded. A controller takes on the ongoing job of comparing the observed state of the cluster against the declared desired state and correcting any discrepancy, for as long as the object exists, reacting to events as they happen. The failure scenario where this matters: a node hosting two of your three replicas crashes at 3 AM. With a one-time deployment script, nothing happens. The script that created those Pods exited hours or days ago, and no process even knows they're gone. With Kubernetes, the ReplicaSet controller notices within seconds that the observed replica count (1) no longer matches the desired count (3) and creates two replacement Pods, with no alert, no on-call page, and no human re-running anything. The declarative model turns infrastructure that has to be operated and re-run when things break into infrastructure that keeps correcting itself toward a declared intent, and everything else in Kubernetes builds on that.

concepts.title: Cluster Architecture and the Control Loop
concepts.description: Every Kubernetes cluster splits into a control plane that watches and decides and worker nodes that run workloads. The mechanism tying every component together is the reconciliation control loop: a continuous cycle of observe, diff, and act that by design never finishes.
learningObjectives: Name the core control plane components (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and describe each one's single responsibility.
Name the core node components (kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy) and describe each one's responsibility.
Describe the generic shape of a Kubernetes control loop: observe actual state, compare to desired state, act to reduce the difference, repeat.
Explain why controllers only communicate through the API server and etcd, and never call each other directly.
Trace what happens end-to-end when kubectl apply creates a new Deployment, from the API server through to a running Pod.
Explain why level-triggered (rather than edge-triggered) reconciliation makes Kubernetes resilient to a controller crashing mid-operation.

sections.heading: The Control Plane: The Cluster's Brain
sections.body:
The control plane is the set of components that make decisions about the cluster's state; it doesn't run your application workloads. Four pieces matter most:

The **API server** is the single entry point for everything. Every `kubectl` command, every controller, and every kubelet talks to the cluster through the API server's REST interface. It authenticates requests, authorizes them (RBAC), runs them through any configured admission webhooks, validates the object, and is the *only* component that talks to etcd. Nothing else in the cluster reads or writes etcd on its own. The API server also exposes a *watch* mechanism that streams changes to clients, which is how controllers and kubelets learn about new or changed objects without polling.

**etcd** is a distributed, consistent key-value store and the source of truth for all cluster state; every object you've applied lives here. It uses the Raft consensus algorithm to stay consistent across replicas, which is why etcd typically runs as an odd-sized cluster (3 or 5 members) rather than a single instance: losing etcd, or losing quorum among its members, means losing the cluster's memory of what should exist. That is why etcd backups (for example `etcdctl snapshot save`) are the core of cluster disaster recovery, and why managed Kubernetes services take that job off your hands.

The **scheduler** watches for Pods that have been created but have no node assigned, and its only job is to pick a suitable node for each one, based on resource requests, affinity/anti-affinity rules, taints and tolerations, and similar constraints. It never starts a container, never talks to a node, and never runs anything. Its output is a node assignment written back to the API server. If no node satisfies a Pod's constraints, the Pod stays Pending and the scheduler retries as the cluster changes.

The **controller manager** is a single binary that bundles the many independent built-in controllers (the Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller, Node controller, and dozens more) for operational convenience. Each runs its own reconciliation loop, watching its own slice of objects, with no awareness of the others' internal logic.

sections.heading: Nodes: Where Work Actually Happens
sections.body:
Every worker node runs a small set of agents whose job is to make that node do what the control plane has decided.

The **kubelet** is the agent on every node, and the only node-level component that talks to the container runtime. It watches the API server for Pods assigned (via `nodeName`) to its own node and runs its own reconciliation loop: which Pods does the API server say belong on me, which containers are running via the runtime right now, and what's the difference? It also reports node and Pod status back to the API server, which is how `kubectl get nodes` and Pod phases (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed) stay accurate.

The **container runtime** (containerd and CRI-O are the common choices today) pulls images and creates, starts, and stops containers at the OS level. Kubernetes talks to it through a standard interface, the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), so Kubernetes doesn't need to know which runtime is underneath; the kubelet issues the same CRI calls regardless.

**kube-proxy** runs on every node and maintains the network rules that let traffic addressed to a Service reach one of the Pods backing it. It gets proper treatment in the Services concept in the next module; for now, place it on the map as a node-level networking component, not a control plane component. (Some clusters replace it with an eBPF-based dataplane such as Cilium's, but Services behave the same from your side.)

sections.heading: The Control Loop Pattern, Generalized
Everything Talks Through the API Server
sections.body:
A detail that seems minor but underpins the system's reliability: the scheduler, the controllers inside controller-manager, and every kubelet never call each other over the network. Each only watches the API server for changes and writes results back to it. The scheduler doesn't open a connection to a kubelet to tell it to run something; it writes a node assignment to the Pod object, and the relevant kubelet discovers it by watching.

This indirection pays off in resilience. If the scheduler crashes and restarts, no other component needs retry or reconnection logic, because nothing held a connection to it. Everything else keeps watching the API server, oblivious to whether the scheduler was up, down, or restarting. Imagine instead a scheduler that called kubelets directly: a kubelet restart, a network partition, or a slow kubelet would each require the scheduler to implement its own handling. Routing everything through one well-defined, highly available choke point (the API server, backed by etcd) avoids N-squared bespoke failure handling between every pair of components.

sections.heading: Tracing kubectl apply End to End
sections.body:
Walking through the full chain once shows how 'independent loops, chained only by what they read and write' behave in practice:

1. `kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml` sends the manifest to the **API server**, which authenticates, authorizes, runs admission webhooks, and persists the Deployment object into **etcd**.
2. The **Deployment controller** (inside controller-manager), which is watching Deployment objects, notices the new/changed Deployment and creates or updates a **ReplicaSet** to match its Pod template.
3. The **ReplicaSet controller**, watching ReplicaSets and Pods independently, notices this ReplicaSet wants N Pods but 0 currently exist matching its selector, and creates N **Pod** objects -- unscheduled, with no `nodeName` set yet.
4. The **scheduler**, watching specifically for Pods with an empty `nodeName`, evaluates each one against available nodes' resources and constraints, and writes a `nodeName` back to the API server (a binding) for each Pod.
5. The **kubelet** on that specific node, watching for Pods now assigned to itself, notices the new Pod and calls the **container runtime** via CRI to pull the image and start the containers.
6. The kubelet reports the Pod's status (eventually `Running`, and separately, `Ready` once probes pass) back to the API server.

No single component in this chain orchestrates the whole sequence, and none of them needs to know the others exist. Each is an independent loop reacting to the narrow slice of state it cares about. The order emerges from data dependencies (a Pod can't be scheduled before it exists or started before it's scheduled), not from any explicit coordination.

examples.title: A Minimal Mental Model of a Controller Loop
examples.explanation: Notice what this loop does *not* do: it never stores 'I created pods X, Y, Z last time' or remembers any history. Every pass reads the current desired replica count and the current Pod count and acts on the difference between those two numbers. That is what 'level-triggered' means in practice, and it's why a controller can crash at any point (mid-loop, mid-create) and restart later with no special recovery logic: it runs the same loop body, recomputes the diff from current reality, and picks up wherever the diff says work remains. There is no in-progress operation to resume, because the loop never tracked 'progress' in the first place, only the gap between desired and actual.

examples.title: Reading the Trace: kubectl get events
examples.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -5

# 12s   Normal   Scheduled   pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Successfully assigned default/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp to node-2
# 11s   Normal   Pulling     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Pulling image "nginx:1.26"
# 9s    Normal   Pulled      pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Successfully pulled image "nginx:1.26" in 1.8s
# 9s    Normal   Created     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Created container nginx
# 8s    Normal   Started     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Started container nginx
examples.explanation: Each event line maps onto a component from the trace above. 'Scheduled' is emitted by the scheduler when it writes a node binding for this Pod. Everything after that comes from the kubelet on node-2 as it makes CRI calls to the container runtime: Pulling and Pulled bracket the image pull, and Created/Started bracket container creation and startup. If a Pod gets stuck, `kubectl describe pod` and this event stream tell you which stage, and therefore which component's loop, isn't making progress. A Pod stuck with no Scheduled event means the scheduler can't find a fit (check resource requests and node capacity). A Pod stuck at Pulling points to an image pull problem (registry auth, network, a typo'd tag) on the kubelet/runtime side; the scheduler finished long before and is irrelevant to that failure.

misconceptions.description: The scheduler creates and starts the Pod on the node it picks -- it's the component 'running' the workload.
misconceptions.clarification: The scheduler's output is a node assignment (nodeName) written into the Pod object via the API server. It never talks to a node and never starts a container. Running the workload is the job of the kubelet and container runtime, as a separate, independent reaction: the kubelet on the chosen node is watching the API server for Pods bound to it, notices the new binding, and only then begins pulling images and starting containers. The scheduler has moved on to other Pods long before any container on that node starts pulling its image.
misconceptions.fact: The scheduler's only output is a node assignment (nodeName) written back into the Pod object via the API server; it never talks to any node directly and never starts a container.

misconceptions.description: The controllers inside controller-manager coordinate by calling each other directly -- for example, the ReplicaSet controller calls into the Deployment controller to know when to act.
misconceptions.clarification: Controllers never call each other, even when they're compiled into the same controller-manager binary. Each is an independent loop that watches the API server for the object kinds it cares about. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet object and is done with that action; the ReplicaSet controller, which has no awareness of the Deployment controller, is watching ReplicaSet objects too and reacts to that ReplicaSet appearing or changing. All coordination between controllers is indirect, mediated by objects persisted in etcd, never by a function call or network request between controllers.
misconceptions.fact: Controllers never call each other directly, even when they're compiled into the same controller-manager binary for operational convenience.

exercises.prompt: You apply a fresh Deployment with 1 replica to an empty namespace on a healthy cluster, and immediately start watching events. For a single Pod, which event Reason will always appear first: 'Scheduled' or 'Started', and why must it happen in that order given which components are responsible for each?
exercises.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get events -w
hints: Which component is responsible for emitting each of those two events -- are they the same component, or two entirely separate ones?
Can the kubelet do anything at all with a Pod before that Pod has a nodeName assigned to it?
This ordering isn't enforced by any orchestrator deciding 'do Scheduled, then do Started' -- it falls out of a hard data dependency between two independent loops.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'Scheduled' always appears first. The kubelet (which emits 'Started' once it starts the container) only ever watches for Pods that already have a nodeName assigned to its own node: it has nothing to act on until the scheduler has written that binding, so Scheduled is a hard prerequisite, not a usual convention.
exercises.solutionExplanation: 'Scheduled' is emitted by the scheduler when it writes a nodeName binding onto the Pod. 'Started' is emitted later by the kubelet on that node, after it has seen the Pod bound to itself, pulled the image via the container runtime, and started the container process. No orchestrator forces this order as policy; it's a data dependency. The kubelet's watch is filtered to Pods already assigned to its node, so it has nothing to react to until a nodeName exists. No amount of speed or luck lets Started happen before Scheduled, because the thing the kubelet reacts to doesn't exist until the scheduler creates it.

exercises.prompt: A Pod has been stuck in `Pending` for over ten minutes on a 3-node cluster where each node has 4 CPUs. `kubectl describe pod web-abc123` shows: `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.` Find and fix the bug in this Pod spec.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-abc123
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.26
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "16"
          memory: "256Mi"
hints: The scheduler will only place a Pod on a node that has enough *unallocated* capacity to satisfy every one of the Pod's resource requests -- what does this Pod's cpu request say it needs, and how does that compare to a single node's total capacity?
'Insufficient cpu' on all 3 nodes simultaneously is a strong signal this isn't about one bad node -- it's a request the cluster as a whole cannot satisfy on any single node.
cpu: "16" means 16 full CPU cores. Reread how many CPUs each node actually has.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-abc123
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.26
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "250m"
          memory: "256Mi"
exercises.solutionExplanation: The Pod requested 16 CPU cores (cpu: "16"), but every node has only 4 CPUs, so no node, even a completely idle one, could satisfy the request. That is what '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu' reports. It's a scheduler-stage failure: the scheduler looks for a node with enough unallocated capacity to cover every resource request on the Pod, and refuses to place the Pod anywhere rather than overcommit a node. The fix lowers the request to something sensible for nginx: 250m (250 millicpu, a quarter of a core), which fits easily on a 4-CPU node. To see how much each node has left, `kubectl describe node <name>` lists Allocatable and Allocated resources. The broader lesson: requests should reflect what the container needs on an ongoing basis, not a large number 'just to be safe'. Oversized requests are a common cause of Pods that never schedule.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the division of responsibility between the Kubernetes scheduler and the kubelet?
options: The scheduler decides which node a Pod should run on; the kubelet on that node is responsible for actually starting the containers via the container runtime.
The kubelet decides which node to run on by querying nearby kubelets for available capacity, and the scheduler merely records that decision afterward in etcd.
The scheduler both selects the node and directly instructs that node's kubelet over a persistent connection to start the containers.
There's no meaningful separation of concerns -- 'scheduler' and 'kubelet' are just two names describing the same control plane process.
assessments.explanation: The scheduler's only output is a node assignment written back to the API server; the kubelet on that node discovers the assignment by watching and is the only component that talks to the container runtime to start containers. The “The kubelet decides which node to run…” option inverts the responsibility: kubelets never negotiate placement with each other, and there is no peer-to-peer capacity query. The “The scheduler both selects the node…” option is wrong on two counts: the scheduler never talks to a kubelet directly, and there is no persistent connection between them, because everything is mediated through the API server. The “There's no meaningful separation of concerns…” option is false: the scheduler and kubelet are separate processes with non-overlapping responsibilities (deciding placement vs. executing it).

assessments.prompt: Why does etcd typically run as a cluster with an odd number of members (3 or 5) rather than an even number like 4?
options: etcd requires an odd number of members so the scheduler and controller-manager can each be pinned to a distinct half of the cluster.

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm, which requires a strict majority (quorum) of members to agree on writes; a 4-member cluster tolerates the same single member failure as a 3-member cluster while needing an extra host to achieve it, so an odd count maximizes fault tolerance per member added.
Odd numbers are required because the API server can only maintain persistent connections to an odd number of backend hosts at a time.
Odd numbers are purely a naming convention with no technical basis; an even-numbered etcd cluster works identically in every respect.
assessments.explanation: Raft quorum is a strict majority. A 3-member cluster needs 2 to agree and tolerates 1 failure; a 4-member cluster needs 3 and still tolerates only 1. The fourth member adds cost and no fault tolerance. A 5-member cluster tolerates 2 failures. That's why etcd deployments favor odd counts: each extra failure tolerated requires moving to the next odd size (3 members tolerate one, 5 tolerate two, 7 tolerate three). None of the other options describe anything etcd, the API server, the scheduler, or controller-manager does.

assessments.prompt: The scheduler process crashes and stays down for two minutes before restarting. During that outage, what happens to the kubelets already running on every node and to the controllers already running inside controller-manager?
options: controller-manager also crashes shortly afterward, since its controllers depend on a direct RPC call to the scheduler on every reconciliation pass.
Every kubelet immediately enters a degraded retry loop, since kubelets require a live TCP connection to the scheduler in order to accept new Pod bindings.
Any Pod that was already scheduled before the crash gets un-scheduled and reverted to Pending until the scheduler comes back online.

They keep running completely normally and are unaffected, because none of them ever held a direct connection to the scheduler in the first place -- they only watch and write to the API server, oblivious to whether the scheduler happens to be up, down, or restarting.
assessments.explanation: This is the payoff of routing every component's communication through the API server: nothing else holds a connection to the scheduler, so nothing needs special handling when it's down. kubelets keep managing already-assigned Pods and watching for new bindings that won't arrive until the scheduler is back; controller-manager's controllers keep reconciling everything unrelated to scheduling. None of the other options are true: there's no kubelet-to-scheduler connection, no controller-manager-to-scheduler RPC dependency, and already-scheduled Pods are never un-scheduled because the scheduler is down.

assessments.prompt: A ReplicaSet controller crashes immediately after creating 1 of the 3 Pods it had determined were needed, then restarts 5 seconds later. Given that Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered rather than edge-triggered, what does it do upon restarting?
options: It re-creates all 3 Pods from scratch, including a duplicate of the one that already exists, resulting in 4 total Pods.
It resumes from a saved checkpoint recording that 1 of 3 Pods was already created, and creates exactly the remaining 2.

It has no memory of the partial work at all; it simply reruns its normal loop, reads the current desired count (3) and the current actual count (1, since one Pod really was created before the crash), computes the same diff of 2, and creates 2 more Pods -- arriving at the correct result with no special crash-recovery logic.
It refuses to act until an administrator manually reconciles the discrepancy, since the controller has no way to know whether the first Pod's creation actually succeeded.
assessments.explanation: Level-triggered reconciliation means the controller never tracks 'progress' through a multi-step operation. Every pass recomputes desired-minus-actual from current reality and acts on the gap. So a mid-operation crash needs no recovery path: on restart the controller runs the same loop body, sees that 1 Pod exists (it was persisted in etcd before the crash), and creates the 2 still missing. The “It resumes from a saved checkpoint recording…” option describes checkpointed, edge-triggered behavior, which controllers avoid; the “It re-creates all 3 Pods from scratch…” and “It refuses to act until an administrator…” options describe failures that a naive edge-triggered design might produce, not the level-triggered one Kubernetes uses.

assessments.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why Kubernetes controllers are designed to react to the current difference between desired and actual state (level-triggered) rather than to the specific sequence of events that produced that difference (edge-triggered), and why this design matters for a system that has to tolerate components crashing and restarting.
assessments.modelAnswer: A level-triggered controller, on every reconciliation pass, ignores history: it re-reads the current desired state and current actual state and acts on whatever difference exists between those two snapshots. An edge-triggered design would react to individual events ('a Pod was just deleted', 'a Pod was just created') and would need to track which events it has handled and what step it was in when it last ran. The level-triggered approach matters in a distributed system where any component can crash and restart at any moment, because every pass is self-contained and idempotent: there's no partial state to recover and no 'was I creating Pod 2 of 3 when I crashed' bookkeeping to reconstruct. If a controller crashes after creating one of three needed Pods and restarts moments later, it reruns its normal loop, sees that actual (1) doesn't match desired (3), and creates the remaining two, the same code path it would have run anyway, with no crash-recovery branch. The same property keeps controllers correct even when an individual watch event is dropped or missed (which can happen over an unreliable network): since the controller relies on re-checking current state rather than having seen every event, a missed event is caught on the next resync instead of causing permanent, undetected drift.

concepts.title: Pods: The Smallest Deployable Unit
concepts.description: A Pod, not a container, is the unit Kubernetes schedules and manages. Before Deployments or Services will make sense, you need to know why Kubernetes wraps containers in this extra layer, what those containers share as a result, and why Pods are treated as disposable rather than repairable.
learningObjectives: Explain why Kubernetes schedules Pods rather than individual containers, and define what a Pod actually is.
Describe what containers within the same Pod share (network namespace, and optionally volumes) and what they do not share by default (PID namespace).
Explain the purpose of init containers versus regular containers, including their ordering and failure-handling guarantees.
Explain why Pods are treated as ephemeral and disposable rather than repaired in place, in contrast to a traditional VM.
Predict what happens to a Pod's IP address and identity when it is deleted and a replacement is created, even from an identical spec.
Describe the sidecar pattern and give a concrete real-world use case for a multi-container Pod.

sections.heading: What Exactly Is a Pod?
sections.body:
A Pod is a group of one or more containers that Kubernetes schedules, starts, and terminates together, as a single unit, on one node. You can't put half a Pod on one node and the other half on another; for scheduling purposes the Pod is indivisible.

Most Pods you'll meet contain one container, and in that common case it's tempting to treat 'Pod' and 'container' as synonyms. They aren't, and the difference matters the moment you need a second, tightly coupled helper that must live and die alongside your main container, share its network identity, and run on the same node: a log shipper, a TLS-terminating proxy, a file synchronizer. The Pod is Kubernetes' answer to 'these processes are inseparable,' so the scheduler never places your app on one node and its required sidecar on another.

sections.heading: What Containers in a Pod Actually Share
sections.body:
Containers within the same Pod share a **network namespace**: they have one Pod IP address between them and one port space. Two containers in the same Pod can't both bind port 8080; the second fails with 'address already in use,' as it would for two processes on one traditional host, because as far as the network stack is concerned that's what they are. Containers in a Pod talk to each other over `localhost`, not the Pod's external IP, since from inside either container's network namespace the other's listening ports are local ports.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
    - name: metrics-sidecar
      image: metrics-exporter:2.1
      ports:
        - containerPort: 9090
```

Containers can also share **volumes**: storage defined once at the Pod level and mounted into any number of its containers. A common pattern is an `emptyDir` volume that one container writes to and another reads from: local disk sharing on whichever node the Pod lands on, with no network call involved.

What containers in a Pod do **not** share by default is the **PID (process) namespace**. Each container keeps its own process tree, so `ps aux` inside container A won't show container B's processes unless the Pod opts in with `shareProcessNamespace: true`. This corrects the natural but wrong assumption that 'sharing a Pod' means 'sharing everything a VM would share': a Pod shares specific namespaces and volumes, not the whole OS-level environment.

sections.heading: Init Containers vs. Main Containers
sections.body:
A Pod can declare `initContainers`, which run to completion, in the order listed, before any of the Pod's regular containers start. If an init container fails, the kubelet restarts it according to the Pod's `restartPolicy`, and none of the regular containers start until every init container has exited successfully. That makes init containers the natural place for sequential setup work: waiting for a dependency to become reachable, running a one-time migration, fetching a config bundle, anything that must finish, in order, before the main application starts. Init containers have their own image, so they can carry tools (`nc`, `git`, a migration CLI) that you don't want in the app image.

```yaml
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
```

Regular containers, by contrast, all start at roughly the same time once init containers finish, with no ordering guarantee among themselves, and they run for the Pod's whole lifetime. A regular container that exists to support the main workload (a log shipper, a proxy, a cache warmer) is informally called a **sidecar**, though structurally it's another entry in the same `containers` list. Recent Kubernetes versions add a formal 'sidecar container' feature: an entry in `initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always` gets defined startup ordering plus a long-running lifecycle. The classic pattern to understand first is simpler: another regular, always-running container in the same Pod.

sections.heading: Pods Are Cattle, Not Pets: Ephemerality and Identity
sections.body:
This is the biggest mental shift coming from VM-based operations. If a container inside a Pod crashes, the kubelet restarts *that container* in place, within the *same* Pod, with the same name and IP, governed by `restartPolicy`. That part feels like restarting a service on a VM.

But if the *Pod itself* is deleted, evicted, or lost along with its node, it is gone for good; there is no 'restarting the Pod.' What you'll see instead, assuming a controller manages the Pod (covered next module), is a *replacement* Pod created fresh: a new name and a new IP address. The replacement isn't a revival of the old Pod; it's a new object built from the same template. Never hardcode, cache, or build automation around a specific Pod's IP surviving anything. The set of backing IPs changes constantly, and Services (next module) exist to paper over that.

One more point: Pods are almost never created directly in production. You can run `kubectl run` and get a bare Pod, and it works until something goes wrong. A bare Pod has no controller watching it, so if it's deleted or its node fails, nothing recreates it. That violates the self-healing premise from the Declarative vs. Imperative concept. In practice Pods are created indirectly through a controller (a Deployment, a StatefulSet, a Job) that supplies the reconciliation loop needed to keep the right number of Pods matching a template in existence, which is the subject of the next module.

examples.title: A Multi-Container Pod Sharing a Volume and a Network Namespace
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: shared-logs
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
    - name: log-shipper
      image: log-shipper:1.2
      volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
          readOnly: true
examples.explanation: Both containers mount the same `emptyDir` volume, `shared-logs`, at the same path. Because they're in the same Pod, on the same node, this is the same directory on that node's filesystem under both of them. The log-shipper can tail files the app writes with no network calls; this works because a Pod's volumes are a Pod-level construct, mounted into whichever of its containers ask for them. Separately, both containers share one network namespace and therefore one IP: if app needed to reach a metrics endpoint the log-shipper exposed on port 9090, it would use `localhost:9090`, not the Pod's external IP, and if app also tried to bind port 9090 the two would conflict, because there is one port space for the whole Pod. Two separate Pods would each get their own.

examples.title: Ephemerality: A Replacement Pod Is Not the Same Pod
examples.code:
kubectl get pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp -o wide
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
# web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp      1/1     Running   10.244.1.14   node-2

kubectl delete pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp
# pod "web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp" deleted

# (Deployment's ReplicaSet controller notices the count dropped and creates a replacement)
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
# web-7d9f8c9b7-9plm2      1/1     Running   10.244.2.31   node-3
examples.explanation: The replacement Pod has a different generated name suffix, a different IP address (10.244.2.31 instead of 10.244.1.14), and even landed on a different node. It is not the original Pod coming back. It's a new object created by the ReplicaSet controller because it saw the actual replica count drop below the desired count, the same reconciliation behavior from the previous concept. Anything that had cached or hardcoded 10.244.1.14 as 'the web Pod's address' is now talking to nothing, with no error to say so. That's why nothing in a healthy Kubernetes setup should address an individual Pod by IP, and it's the gap a Service's stable virtual IP closes, which is where the next module picks up. You can watch it happen with `kubectl get pods -l app=web -w` while deleting a Pod: the old name terminates and a new one appears within seconds.

misconceptions.description: A Pod is basically just Kubernetes' name for a single container -- in casual conversation 'Pod' and 'container' mean the same thing, and that's fine because in practice they usually are the same thing.
misconceptions.clarification: The common one-container-per-Pod case creates that illusion, but a Pod is a distinct scheduling and resource-sharing boundary that can hold multiple containers sharing one network namespace and, optionally, volumes. The conflation breaks down when you meet any sidecar pattern, when you reason about restartPolicy (which applies at the Pod level, to every container inside it), or when you ask why two containers in the same Pod can't bind the same port. That constraint has nothing to do with containers in general and everything to do with the Pod-level network namespace they share.

misconceptions.description: If a Pod is deleted -- whether by a person, an eviction, or a node failure -- Kubernetes 'heals' it by restarting that exact same Pod object in place, preserving its identity and IP, like rebooting a VM.
misconceptions.clarification: Container-level restart and Pod-level replacement are two different mechanisms. When one container inside a Pod crashes, the kubelet restarts that container in place, within the same Pod and with the same IP, which does resemble a VM reboot. But once the Pod object itself is deleted or evicted, it is gone; there is no repair-in-place for a whole Pod. If something is watching the count (a ReplicaSet), it creates a brand-new Pod object with a new name and new IP rather than resurrecting the old one. Treating a Pod's IP as durable across this kind of event is a common source of production bugs.

exercises.prompt: This Pod defines two containers that both try to bind port 8080. What happens when the Pod is created, and why is this fundamentally different from two separate Pods each trying to bind port 8080 on the same node?
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: port-conflict
spec:
  containers:
    - name: server-a
      image: my-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
    - name: server-b
      image: my-other-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
hints: How many network namespaces does this single Pod have in total -- one shared by both containers, or one per container?
Binding a port twice within a single network namespace behaves the same way it would for two ordinary processes on one traditional host.
Think about whether Kubernetes would even reject this at apply time, or whether the failure happens later, inside one of the running containers.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Kubernetes accepts the manifest: there's no validation against duplicate containerPort declarations. But at runtime, whichever container's process tries to bind port 8080 second will fail with an 'address already in use' error, because both containers share exactly one network namespace and therefore one port space for the whole Pod. That container will likely crash-loop. Two separate Pods each binding 8080 would have no conflict at all, because each Pod gets its own independent network namespace and IP.
exercises.solutionExplanation: containerPort in a Pod spec is documentation for humans and tooling; it doesn't reserve the port or prevent a collision, and Kubernetes doesn't validate that two containers in a Pod use different ports. The conflict happens at the OS level, inside whichever container's process calls bind(8080) second within the shared network namespace, and it fails the way two ordinary processes on one host would. Depending on restartPolicy, the kubelet will likely keep restarting the failing container, producing a CrashLoopBackOff. Two separate Pods, each with its own network namespace and IP, could both bind port 8080 with no conflict, because the port space is scoped per Pod, not per node or cluster.

exercises.prompt: This Pod is meant to wait for a database to become reachable before the app container starts, but both containers start at the same time, creating a race condition where the app sometimes fails to connect. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
hints: All entries under `containers:` start together, with no ordering guarantee between them -- is that really what should be true for a container whose entire purpose is to run and finish BEFORE anything else?
Kubernetes has a dedicated field for containers that must run to completion, strictly in order, before any regular container starts.
The fix is about which list this container belongs to, not about changing its command.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original spec, wait-for-db sat under `containers`, so it starts at roughly the same time as app with no guarantee it finishes, or even starts, before app tries to connect to the database. That's the race. Moving it into `initContainers` changes its behavior: init containers run to completion in the order listed, and the kubelet won't start any regular container until every init container has exited successfully (exit code 0). Now `app` can't start until wait-for-db's loop has detected that the database is reachable and exited, which removes the race by construction instead of relying on timing.

assessments.prompt: Two containers, A and B, are defined in the same Pod spec with no special namespace-sharing options set. Which of these is something they share by default?
options: The same container image, so both containers necessarily run identical code.
The same root filesystem, so a file written by container A at /tmp/data.txt is automatically visible to container B at the same path.
The same network namespace, so they share one Pod IP and can reach each other over localhost.
The same PID (process) namespace, so `ps aux` inside container A shows container B's processes too.
assessments.explanation: Containers in the same Pod share a network namespace by default: one Pod IP, one port space, and localhost reachability, which is why two containers in one Pod can't bind the same port. The “The same PID (process) namespace, so ps…” option is false by default: PID namespaces are isolated per container unless the Pod sets shareProcessNamespace: true. The “The same root filesystem, so a file…” option is false: each container has its own root filesystem from its own image, and only declared shared volumes (like emptyDir) are visible across containers, at the paths where each mounts them. The “The same container image, so both containers…” option is false: a Pod's containers usually come from different images serving different purposes, such as an app and a sidecar.

assessments.prompt: A Pod defines two init containers, `fetch-config` and `run-migration`, listed in that order, followed by one regular container `app`. If `fetch-config` fails (a non-zero exit code) and the Pod's restartPolicy is `Always`, what happens?
options: The kubelet restarts `fetch-config` according to the restartPolicy; `run-migration` and `app` will not start until `fetch-config` eventually exits successfully, because init containers run strictly in the order listed and none of the regular containers start until every init container has completed successfully.
`run-migration` and `app` start immediately anyway, since init container failures are only logged as warning events and never block anything.
The kubelet skips `fetch-config` after one failed attempt and proceeds directly to `run-migration`, since init containers are treated as best-effort by design.
The whole Pod object is permanently deleted the moment any init container fails, forcing a controller to create an entirely new Pod.
assessments.explanation: Init containers are an ordered gate: each must exit successfully before the next init container, or once all are done the regular containers, may start. A failing init container is restarted according to the Pod's restartPolicy, like a regular container, and nothing downstream of it (neither run-migration nor app) starts until it succeeds. There's no best-effort skipping and no automatic deletion of the Pod because an init container failed; the Pod stays not-Ready, retrying the failed init container with backoff, until it succeeds or someone intervenes.

assessments.prompt: A developer runs `kubectl run debug-pod --image=busybox` to get a bare Pod with no owning Deployment, ReplicaSet, or other controller. The node it lands on is later drained and removed from the cluster. What happens to debug-pod?
options: The API server itself detects the orphaned Pod and re-creates it as a built-in safety default, independent of any controller.
The kubelet on whichever node it would have been rescheduled to automatically adopts it, preserving its original name and IP.
A replacement Pod is automatically created on a different node, exactly as if it had been managed by a Deployment, because the scheduler itself tracks and re-places all Pods regardless of ownership.
debug-pod is gone permanently, and nothing recreates it -- a bare Pod has no controller running a reconciliation loop that would notice its absence and act on it, so it simply stays deleted.
assessments.explanation: Self-healing in Kubernetes isn't a property of Pods. It comes from a controller's reconciliation loop noticing that the observed count no longer matches a declared desired count and acting on the gap. A bare Pod has no such controller and no ReplicaSet declaring 'there should be one of these,' so when it's lost with its node, nothing notices or recreates it. That's why Pods are almost never created directly in production: they're created through a Deployment, StatefulSet, or Job to get that reconciliation guarantee, which a bare Pod lacks. (kubectl drain also refuses to evict a bare Pod unless you force it.)

assessments.prompt: A single container inside a running, multi-container Pod crashes due to an unhandled exception, while the rest of the Pod is unaffected. Assuming a normal restartPolicy, what happens to the Pod's identity (its name and IP address) as a result?
options: The Pod's IP changes but its name stays the same, because IP addresses are reassigned to a Pod every time any of its containers restart, for security isolation.
The kubelet restarts just that one container in place, within the same Pod object -- the Pod keeps its original name and IP throughout.
The whole Pod is deleted and a brand-new Pod is created with a new name and new IP, since any single container's failure is treated as a failure of the entire Pod.
Nothing restarts automatically at all; a human must manually delete the Pod before any controller will create a working replacement.
assessments.explanation: This is the distinction between container-level restart and Pod-level replacement. When one container in a Pod crashes, the kubelet restarts that container in place, within the same Pod object, and the Pod's name and IP are unaffected because the Pod was never deleted; only one process inside it was. Replacement with a new name and IP happens only when the Pod object itself is deleted, evicted, or lost with its node, which is a different scenario, driven by a controller creating a fresh Pod rather than by the kubelet's container-restart behavior.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a Pod, not an individual container, is the smallest unit Kubernetes actually schedules and manages, and describe specifically what would break if Kubernetes instead scheduled and scaled containers independently of one another.
assessments.modelAnswer: Kubernetes schedules Pods because some units of deployable work need more than one container acting as a single, inseparable thing, most commonly a main application container plus a tightly coupled helper like a log shipper or proxy sidecar. Both need to be on the same node, share a network identity, and rise and fall together. The Pod is the abstraction for that: the boundary the scheduler treats as atomic (never splitting a Pod's containers across nodes), the boundary that defines one shared network namespace and IP (so sidecars reach the main container over localhost with no network hop), and the boundary that defines optional shared volumes for local data exchange. If Kubernetes scheduled and scaled individual containers independently, several things would break. A sidecar could land on a different node from the container it supports, defeating colocated helpers. There would be no natural way to give a pair of tightly coupled containers one IP and localhost reachability, since each container would need its own network identity. And scaling would become incoherent: if 'scale to 3' meant three independent containers rather than three copies of a coupled group, nothing would guarantee matched app-and-sidecar pairs, only however many of each happened to be scheduled. The Pod makes 'these containers are inseparable, so treat them as one unit for scheduling, networking, and lifecycle' an explicit concept instead of something every user hand-rolls.
